strings.text: Small Things Like These

A small Irish town by a river, the week before Christmas. Bill Furlong delivers coal to the convent on the hill, and one morning finds a girl locked in its coal shed. What will he do for her — and what will it cost his own house?
The coal shed’s bolt is drawn from the outside, and a girl has spent the night on the coal: what will a decent man do for her, and what will it cost him?
after the novella by Claire Keegan
Coal
The barefoot boy
Stop, give him the coins
Drive on
The girl in the chapel
“Wrong door” — and go
His name, and toffees
Ask aloud
In truth: the main street in the morning; Mrs Kehoe in the door of her café; at the end of the street, the hill and the convent, steam over its wall.
Bill drives his lorry out of the yard. Mrs Kehoe in the door of her café nods up at the hill:
Going up there today? Tell them my pie’s better than theirs
In truth: the road out of town, seen from the lorry’s cab.
In the cab, on the dashboard, a child’s drawing: five girls and a lorry. By the roadside a boy is dragging a bundle of sticks — barefoot on the frost.
He can’t give him a lift: the back is full, and the boy is going the other way. At home there are five, every coin counted, and the sisters don’t like him late. And the boy is barefoot.
Stop and give him the coins
Drive on: you’re late as it is
The boy stands with the coins in his palm and watches the lorry go.
In the mirror the boy picks up his sticks.
In truth: the convent chapel — a long floor, girls on their knees with buckets, in thin dresses; the laundry roaring behind the wall.
Bill has tipped the coal; there is no one at the shed, and the docket must be signed. He goes looking for a sister and opens the wrong door.
Girls on their knees scrub the floor, in nothing but their dresses. All of them on their knees; he in the doorway.
One of them has stood up — barefoot, her hands red. Close, her face:
Mister, take me away. Just as far as the river. I can do anything
He can’t take her now, and it shows: a sister is near, it is broad day, she is barefoot.
Say he has the wrong door, and go
Whisper his name, and set a bag of toffees on her bucket
Ask the sister aloud: “Why are they on their knees in this cold?”
She goes down on her knees again. A sister shows him out politely and signs the docket.
My name’s Bill. I come Thursdays, with the coal
She covers the bag with her palm and hides it in her sleeve.
Why are they on their knees in this cold?
Work purifies, Mr Furlong
All the girls look at him. At the end of the corridor stands the Mother Superior; Bill does not see her.
Silence. The cab: Bill’s hand straightens the drawing on the dashboard and stays on it. The engine, the river.
The Furlongs’ kitchen, evening. Sheila at the window sings “Silent Night”.
Sister said whoever sings it best gets the solo at midnight Mass
Loretta writes her letter to Santa, covering it with her hand. Eileen counts the coins in the tin.
At the end Bill eats a cherry himself.
Grace, that’s enough
Eileen counts the coins again.
Again?
Who to, Daddy?
A boy. He’d no shoes
Five of them. And each one will have a present, if you give nothing more away
It’s right
And for the first time this evening she smiles at him.
Five of them. And each one will have a present
And Mary Dougherty sings in her daddy’s socks. Her shoes have holes, you can hear them squelch
Sheila
Kathleen looks over Loretta’s shoulder — Loretta throws herself over the letter:
Don’t look!
Eileen wraps the first cake in paper — not the smallest — and sets it by the door.
That’s for the widow Howie. Since you’re giving her the coal as well
The Shed
“Aren’t you going to ask where he is?”
“I’ll ask where he is”
Say nothing
“They locked me in by mistake”
“The bolt was drawn from the outside”
Let it pass
Sara goes
“Some shoes for her”
The envelope
Take it, for the girls
Take it, for shoes for her
Leave it on the table
Sunday, still dark, frost. On Saturday evening the sisters rang: the coal had run out before the holiday wash. Bill has come before light, to be back in time for Mass with his family.
Close: his key on its ring turns in the coal gate, as always. The shed’s bolt is drawn from the outside, and frozen.
He lifts his lantern: inside, on the coal, sits a girl in a nightgown, barefoot, black with coal dust; the light on her face. The one from the chapel. She has spent the night here.
You’re Bill. Thursdays
Are there any toffees left?
He takes off his coat; cut — the coat is on her.
Come into the warm
She looks past him, at the laundry windows.
I asked where my boy is. Twice
He nods at the lorry beyond the gate — she steps back into the shed.
They’d only bring me back
And, looking at him:
Aren’t you going to ask where he is?
She shrinks.
I’m the coal man
I came for coal. For the kitchen

Quickly, at the floor, with a smile. He holds out his coat — she won’t take it. He lays it on the coal beside her and turns to the bolt; cut — the coat is on her. He nods at the lorry — she shakes her head and steps back. Then, past him, as if to no one:
I only asked where my boy is
I’ll ask where he is
She nods, not believing him.
She nods, as if she had thought as much, and looks at the windows.
Over the yard the bell rings for work: six. Sara gets up by herself before she knows she has — habit is stronger than fear.
Not across the yard
She leads him to the kitchen’s back door. The cook nods Sara to a bench and goes upstairs. A minute later the Mother Superior comes down.
Mr Furlong. Come through to me. Sara, you too
That is how he learns her name.
A fire, a ticking clock; the laundry can’t be heard here. The Mother at the window; Bill in the low armchair with a cup of tea; Sara by the door, barefoot, in his coat.
You took an interest in our girls in the chapel, Mr Furlong
She asks after his daughters, each by name; she knows Sheila wants the solo.
Sister Bernadette says the coal was wet last time. Wet coal weighs heavier, Mr Furlong
I’ll take it off, Mother
A pause. The clock.
Sara, tell Mr Furlong how you came to be in the shed
Before she answers, Sara raises her eyes to him for a second and drops them: to ask here would be to have her locked up again. He does not ask.
We were playing hide-and-seek, Mother. They locked me in by mistake
An interruption, to be
On “by mistake” a sign shows at the top of the screen for three seconds: a bolt, and under it his words, “The bolt was outside.”
Tapped — the words break out of Bill. Not tapped — the sign goes. For now: the choice.
“The bolt was drawn from the outside, Mother”
Let the sign pass
The bolt was drawn from the outside, Mother
He puts down the cup and stands; she does not turn from the window. The clock.
All the more reason for us to find out who did it. Sara, go
In the doorway Sara looks back — not gratefully: frightened. What has he done. Through the window he sees her led not to the refectory but down another corridor.
“She could do with some kind of shoes, Mother”
Go on, you’ll be fed
Sara does not look at him.
She could do with some kind of shoes, Mother
Of course. We have everything
Sister Bernadette will keep an eye on her, since you ask for her
In the doorway Sara looks back at him — quick, angry.
Cut: the coat lies on the chair by the door; Sara is gone. Bill gets up to leave. The Mother at the window; behind her, steam over the laundry.
The town brings them to us itself, Mr Furlong. Where would they be, if not here?
The clock. She comes from the window and lays on the table an envelope with a Christmas card; there is money inside.
For your girls
I was one of nine myself. I know what Christmas is
The clock, louder than ever.
Take it: “For the girls, at Christmas”
Take it — and spend it on shoes for her
Thank you, Mother
From now on the envelope lies on the dashboard.
Aloud, the same thanks: she does not know what the money will go on. On Monday — a box from the shoe shop on the lorry’s seat.
The girls have all they need, Mother
She does not take the envelope up until he has gone.
The yard, steam from the laundry windows.
It was Sunday. In the laundry they were working
In the cab Bill opens the card, counts the money and puts it away without looking.
In truth: the porch of the Furlongs’ house; Kathleen in her coat with the little ones.
We’ll be late because of you. Mammy said to wait
Go on, then. You’re not babies
Sharp, not raising his voice; he has never spoken to her like that. Kathleen takes the little ones off without looking back. Bill looks at his black hands.
Home
Eileen: “What’s it to do with us?”
Tell her everything
“We’ll take her in”
Ask for a bundle
“It’s not our business”
Mrs Kehoe: “Mind yourself”
“I only bring the coal”
Ask about her boy
Say it in front of people
In truth: the office in Furlong’s coal yard, Tuesday; the order book.
The convent’s Christmas order is doubled. Bill writes in the line.
You’re their favourite, Bill. What did you do to please them?
The other man laughs. Bill goes off to the scales.
A note from the convent. The narrator reads it:
“The Christmas order of coal has been given to another supplier. The weekly order as before.”
Bill crosses out the line.
We’ll get a rest, anyway
The kitchen, evening; the cake is baking.
Sheila whirls round the kitchen, arms out:
They gave me the solo! Mary Dougherty will cry!
And from the stairs:
Sister said to say hello to Daddy
Don’t gloat
— and smiles herself. Bill puts down the spoon.
They put me out of the choir. I didn’t do anything!
Through her tears — to him:
You bring them their coal. Tell them!
He says nothing.
Eileen looks at Bill a long time.
Kathleen, without asking, carries in a box from the lorry.
Daddy, is this for me? For under the tree?
No, love
Then who?
He says nothing. Close: her own shoe by the door, the sole coming away.

She puts the box on a chair so that the lid flies off onto the floor; at the bang she turns on the stairs — inside, grown-up shoes, brown, with red laces — and goes up, loud on every step. Eileen picks the lid up off the floor. Looks at the price.
The girls go up to bed. Eileen sits down opposite him: both at the table, their hands on it between them.
Her hand on the box:
And what money is this?
The sisters gave it. For Christmas
Gave it for the girls
They tell me you sat half an hour with the Mother Superior on Sunday. Two nights now you haven’t slept. What’s up there?
There was a girl locked in the coal shed all night. Barefoot
What’s it to do with us? Our girls are all right
And quieter, pettily:
I always said Maggie Reilly thought too much of herself. And now her daughter’s gone “to an aunt”
He can’t go to the priest or the guards: the sisters and the town are one.
Her feet were bare. The bolt was on the outside. They took her boy. I can’t leave it so
Eileen gets up and goes to the range, her back to him. A long while.
And did you think of Sheila? Of Joan?
So that’s what Sheila was for
She cries at the range, but she doesn’t leave the kitchen.
She doesn’t touch the box.
Father Murphy has his dinner with them every Sunday
We’ll take her in, the way Mrs Wilson took Mammy. If the sisters give her up
You’re out of your mind
She looks at his hands. Gets up and moves the cake tin.
So you’ve bought her shoes already
She puts the box up on top of the dresser.
If they give her up themselves
She counts on her fingers, aloud, a long time.
She’ll sleep in the pantry. Not a word about her own business in front of the girls. If I hear of it, I’ll take her back myself
She’s my people. From Wexford
And from the range:
Not before Christmas Eve. The pantry’s to be cleared
After what they did to Sheila, you’d go begging to them?
Silence.
You will. You’ll say we need a girl in the house for the holidays. Let them see we’re no enemies of theirs. On Christmas Eve
Would you put up a bundle for me. Socks, a cardigan. For a girl
Eileen looks at him a long time and doesn’t ask: she chooses not to know. She packs the bundle with her back to him.
The box she sets beside the bundle, without opening it.
Give it on Christmas Eve
All that evening she doesn’t raise her eyes to him.
It’s not our business. You’re right
Eileen breathes out, lays her floury palm over his hand — and gets up to the cake.
Kathleen, then. They’re her size, she’ll grow into them
She writes “Kathleen” on the lid and puts the box under the tree.
A warm evening. At night he doesn’t sleep.
In truth: the bridge at night; Bill at the rail under its lamp; fog over the river, the convent on the hill, a light in one window.
Silence. The river. Fifteen seconds.
In truth: Mrs Kehoe’s café, Wednesday morning — the counter, three tables; two men and the postman at one; behind her shoulder a photograph.
Behind Mrs Kehoe’s shoulder hangs a photograph: two girls at a fair, and along its edge, in ink, “Nora and May. The Fair, ’45.”
May, the usual
She leans over the counter, her eyes on the men:
They say you were up there before light on Sunday. Mind yourself, Bill. They’ve a finger in every pie
“I only bring the coal, Mrs Kehoe. I’ve five girls”
Whisper: ask her cousin at the hospital about Sara’s boy
Say it, low: “A girl was locked in the coal shed all night. Barefoot”
I only bring the coal, Mrs Kehoe. I’ve five girls
Then bring it
Without a word she puts an extra pie in his bag.
You’ve a cousin at the county hospital. Find out about a girl’s boy. Sara. The one who was in the shed on Sunday
Mrs Kehoe goes pale. Close: she looks at the photograph. A long time. Wipes the counter.
Mary scrubs their floors. Everything there goes through them. Ask — and they’ll be told someone was asking
Don’t name me
When he goes out, she turns the sign on the door to “Closed”. In the middle of the day.
A girl was locked in the coal shed all night. Barefoot
The table goes quiet. The men look into their cups; the postman puts on his cap and leaves.
Bill, your tea’s getting cold. Who’s for more pie?
Louder than she need. She turns her back to the photograph; her hands shake over the pie.
Close: Bill takes off his scarf and wraps in it what he has brought — the shoes, and Eileen’s socks and cardigan.
Close: Bill takes off his scarf and wraps the shoes in it.
Close: Bill takes off his scarf and wraps in it Eileen’s socks and cardigan.
Close: Bill takes off his scarf. He has nothing to wrap in it: in the scarf there is only the scarf.
The slip of paper stays in his fingers over the scarf longer than it need. He pushes it into a sock.
The slip of paper stays in his fingers over the scarf longer than it need. He pushes it into a shoe.
The slip of paper stays in his fingers over the scarf longer than it need. He folds it into the scarf.
He opens the hatch of the chute — the same one he tips the sacks into — and the bundle goes down with a rustle of coal. Silence.
Bill?
He locks the gate and goes.
The door is open. Close: Sara’s face.
Her hair is cropped. The narrator says nothing.
Cut: his coat is on her shoulders.
His shoes on her feet.
Eileen’s cardigan under the coat.
In the windows of the dormitory, faces: the girls look at the open door and do not come out.
He doesn’t hide her: he leads her out through the gate, down past the main gates, under the lamp, into the town.
By the lodge stands the suitcase. At the gates Sara slows by a step — and goes on, faster than him.
He locks the gate and goes down the hill. At the turn he looks back: the gate in the lamplight. Bells.
Christmas Eve
The coal gate
The bundle down the chute
Ask for her at the main gates
Open the shed
Go home
The coal gate again
In truth: Furlong’s coal yard at noon on Christmas Eve; a paper garland on the scales.
On Thursday he took the sisters their coal, as always. The shed stood open and empty
At the gates a strange lorry was unloading, with the Christmas order
That Thursday: across the yard goes Sara, in convent boots too big for her, a sister a step behind her. She does not raise her eyes.
A paper garland on the scales. Bill lays out the bonus envelopes on them; the men take their own.
The envelopes are thinner — he cut them himself. A man weighs his on his palm:
They took the Christmas order off us. So there’s the bonus
They’re saying in town you were talking about the sisters in the café. So there’s the bonus
The other looks at Bill and says nothing.
The envelopes are as fat as every year; the men joke.
Bill puts the week’s takings in his inside pocket — for Eileen.
The shoebox is already on the lorry’s seat: he took it this morning; Eileen saw, and didn’t ask.
Mrs Kehoe brings the men their pies, as every year. In front of him she sets a bag of pies on the scales and, not looking at him:
They came to Mary. Asking who’d been asking
She goes without looking back. Under the top pie, a folded slip of paper. The narrator reads it:
“Redmond, Sara. A boy, July. In the county home till spring. Then to a family.”
That is how he learns her surname.
Mrs Kehoe brings the men their pies, as every year, and nods to him.
The pies are brought, as every year — but by her nephew:
Auntie’s busy
Sheila runs into the yard with the white choir dress on a hanger:
Daddy, we go at eleven! Sit where you can see me
Grace runs into the yard, a raisin in her cheek:
Mammy says everyone to Mass at eleven. Sheila’s crying she won’t go
I’ll come
Bill washes his hands in the basin.
Close: on the dashboard, the child’s drawing.
Beside it, the sisters’ envelope.
Beside it, the shoebox.
Beside it, Eileen’s bundle.
In truth: the road along the river in a white fog; a fork, and by it a farm with smoke from the chimney.
Bill drives to the house where he grew up, not knowing himself why. At the fork the road can’t be seen.
Out of the farm runs the same boy and silently holds his palm up to the cab window. Bill winds the glass down — cut: the last coin is in the boy’s palm.
Out of the fog comes an old man:
This road will take you wherever you want
In truth: the gate of the old Wilson house behind its trees; the new tenant at the gate.
Ned? He’s in the county home. Since the stroke
In passing:
You’re like him, you know. I thought you’d have been told
He holds out an old hammer, its handle worn down to another man’s palm.
His. Take it, it’s no use to me
And lays it on the gatepost.
The narrator says nothing. Silence: the yard of the house, the stable, the empty window where the kitchen was.
The lorry won’t start in the frost.
My son-in-law will give you a push in the morning. If he’s slept it off
Bill takes what lies on the dashboard and goes on foot. The road into town runs along the convent wall.
Dusk, frost. The bells call to vespers; the streets empty. The laundry is silent.
With the bundle, or for the bargain, he was coming here anyway.
He would only have walked past.
Through the grille, the shed: the bolt is drawn, as it was then.
Across the yard a sister late for vespers carries a small suitcase to the lodge by the main gates, and says to the portress:
Redmond. After midnight Mass
They both go into the lodge. The yard is empty.

From the shed, a cough. Bill stops. The key in the gate, as every Thursday; he goes in and stands at the shed door. His hand in his pocket finds the child’s drawing. From below, from the square, the bell of the church where the choir sings at eleven.
Close: his face, a few seconds, without words.
From the shed, in a whisper, at his steps (the young sister brings her bread):
Sister? Is it bread?
Mr Furlong
They cut my hair. For your bolt
No. It’s you, Bill. I know your step
Who’s there?
The coal man
I’m here by myself. It’s quiet here
Tonight, to Dublin. There’s new sisters there. I’ll ask there
And you never did ask
I asked again. You said…
A cough, and quieter, as if to herself:
I won’t go to Dublin
The yard is empty: the sisters at vespers or in the lodge, the girls locked in the house at this hour. Close: his hand on the bolt. His hands remember it.
He locks the gate, goes down to the main gates and rings. The portress goes for the Mother; the Mother Superior comes to the grille, a shawl about her shoulders.
I don’t think so, Mr Furlong. Happy Christmas
The door closes. He is at the coal gate again.
She’s being moved tonight. Someone in the town was asking about her child. You wouldn’t know who?
Bill says nothing. She looks at him a long time, then at the suitcase by the lodge.
This house lives on donations, Mr Furlong. Like any house
She looks up, at the shed:
She’s being moved. After the holiday
This house lives on donations, Mr Furlong
Bill takes out the week’s takings: the envelope’s money went on the shoes.
Bill takes the money out of the envelope; the card he keeps in his pocket.
Close: white fingers take the money from his palm.
Without turning round, to the portress:
Take the suitcase back
She’s nothing more to ask about now, has she, Mr Furlong?
He unwinds his scarf:
Only that she’d be in the warm tonight, Mother
She wants for nothing, Mr Furlong. Tomorrow, at the coal gate. With your wife
The scarf in his fist. He gives way. From above, from the shed, a cough.
The coal gate again. From the shed, a cough. His hand on the bolt.
On the shelf the neighbours’ Christmas cards stand crowded.
On the shelf, only a few of the neighbours’ cards.
In truth: the main street, lit for Christmas; people coming from vespers. Sara in his coat.
Through the Town
Bill Furlong, are you in your right mind?
He, not looking, to no purpose:
I’ll bring you round a sack. After the holiday
People nod, and don’t stop.
People cross to the other side of the street.
People cross to the other side of the street. Mr Kenny crosses too, looking away.
Mrs Kehoe at her café window watches them, not drawing the curtain; then puts out the light.
Mrs Kehoe draws the curtain of her café.
The café is shut for the holiday.
At the turn he says:
He’s alive. In the home till spring
She stops — and then goes on by herself, ahead of him.
From the pocket of the coat on her shoulders sticks the edge of the sisters’ Christmas card.
In truth: the Furlongs’ house, from the street; Sara beside Bill (the kitchen has no figure of her yet).
By the house they stop.
The kitchen window: warm, the girls’ shadows, the wireless loud.
The kitchen window: warm, the wireless low.
The kitchen window: one lamp, the wireless off.
Sheila is already in her white choir dress, though midnight Mass is five hours off.
Eileen has been coming to the window all evening. She sees them from the street and opens the door before he can knock.
Daddy, you’ll come at eleven?
— and she sees Sara. Eileen looks over their heads at the hill and the convent, not at her daughter:
Take it off. You’re not going tonight
They gave me the solo!
She howls, pulls off the dress (cut: in her house clothes, the dress on its hook) and runs upstairs.
Sheila on the stairs, asking no one:
Is it because of her they put me out?
No one answers.
Upstairs
To the girls; they sit on the stairs and look through the banisters. To Sara and to him:
Well, what are you standing there for. Come in, it’s cold
Upstairs. All of you
Not turning round. She looks at Sara’s feet, not at her face.
Come in
To him, nothing. She goes to the range, her back turned, and leaves the door open.
Kathleen stands in the kitchen door with a tea towel and looks Sara up and down:
Is that the one from the laundry? Is she sleeping here?
Put the kettle on
Kathleen does, loudly.
Seeing the cropped hair, Eileen looks away.
Bill puts Ned’s hammer on the shelf by the wireless.
Last shot: Bill’s hands and Sara’s at the range — one pair black, one red.
Eileen has been waiting for his answer from the sisters: her shadow by the table. She doesn’t come to the window.
Eileen doesn’t come to the window.
No one opens the door.
Sheila at the window, her forehead to the glass, waves to him: she has seen her father, and hasn’t yet made out who is with him.
He goes up to the door; Sara one step below.
Last shot: his hand on the door, not yet open; in his other hand, Ned’s hammer; behind the glass, the white dress.
Last shot: his hand on the door, not yet open; in his other hand, Ned’s hammer; behind the glass, one lamp.
The hardest part was still ahead. But the worst thing he could have done, he had not done
In truth: Christmas Day, the Furlongs’ table; Sara serves at it (the kitchen has no figure of her yet).
The Paper Crown
The Christmas table. Sara, in Kathleen’s old dress, serves; through the open pantry door, a camp bed. Eileen doesn’t hurt her, but speaks to her as to a servant. To a neighbour at the window:
My people. From Wexford
Kathleen knows the shoes under the table and says nothing all dinner; she gets up first and puts her plate in the sink, loudly.
Sheila, hoarse, tells how she sang the solo.
The sisters’ Christmas card — empty, the money gone out of it — stands on the shelf among the neighbours’ cards.
Eileen over the empty tin:
— and counts on her fingers what they’ll live on in January.
In truth: the same Christmas table in the Furlongs’ kitchen.
Loretta pushes a cracker at Sara and nods at her father.
Cut: a paper crown on Sara — and for the first time, Sara laughs.
The crown sits on her cropped hair.
Why is her hair like a boy’s?
Eat
Sara sets a dish beside Bill and coughs into her sleeve; nobody mentions the cough.
Bill…
— and, catching Eileen’s eye:
Mr Furlong. Would you know where my…
Mr Furlong. Would you know…
Eileen raises her eyes: her condition — not a word in front of the girls.
Eat, Sara. Sit down and eat
The slip of paper is in his breast pocket; he doesn’t take it out.
His scarf on the hook by the door.
Last shot: her red hands set a dish on the cloth; his black ones lie flat either side of his plate and do not move.
Sara lived with the Furlongs until spring. In the house, the boy was not spoken of
In truth: the square after midnight Mass; opposite, the convent’s main gates, the lamp over them, frost. The Furlongs come out of the church.
The File behind the Grille
Christmas night, after midnight Mass. Close, from the church: Ned’s hammer on Bill’s knees.
Behind the grille the girls are led in file, with candles, from the chapel to the house — close to the bars, under the lamp.
She is not in the file: the shed was not opened.
His look goes along the faces to the end, and on, up along the wall, to the lamp over the coal gate. It is dark there, and quiet.
What he put down the chute stayed with her in the shed.
His look goes along the faces to the end, and on — to a car by the lodge, its headlights on. Sara is led out of the coal gate above, a sister with a lantern beside her.
At the car, under the lamp, two steps from the Furlongs.
On her feet, his shoes.
On her feet, the convent boots.
Her feet are bare.
The slip of paper in her fist.
Her hair is cropped.
The sister looks at the shoes, then across the square at the Furlongs, and says nothing. Kathleen knows the shoes, turns away and goes on ahead, to her mother.
Sara looks back while the sister opens the car door.
She gets in without looking back.
The car goes off down the street.
Sheila, hoarse after the solo, carries the choir dress over her arm and shows everyone where she tore the hem.
Sheila, put out of the choir, walks beside Eileen and doesn’t look at the file.
By the gates Eileen slows her step.
By the gates Eileen looks at him; he shakes his head. Close: her hands tie Loretta’s scarf tighter.
Eileen looks at the gates and asks nothing.
Eileen doesn’t look at the gates.
They walk side by side; under her breath Eileen tells him about the solo.
They walk together, without a word.
Eileen walks ahead with the little ones; Bill behind, with Kathleen.
On the square Mr Kenny raises his hat and stops to wish them a happy Christmas.
On the square Mr Kenny nods and walks on.
No scarf: his neck bare in the frost. Loretta, asleep on her feet, drops a mitten. Close: the mitten in his hand.
Last shot: Bill’s black hand round Loretta’s small mitten.
On Thursday he took the sisters their coal. The shed stood open and empty
The Misted Glass
The kitchen, the evening of Christmas Eve. Bill comes in from the cold and puts on the chair by the door what he brought back.
Eileen doesn’t ask where he’s been. She puts out his plate.
Well, what did the sisters say?
They don’t think so
Not today
She turns away to the range: it’s easier for her, and she is ashamed of it.
She sees the bundle on the chair by the door and says nothing.
